items.actClause: AN ACT relating to redistributing 2009 bond volume allocations made pursuant to section 146 of the federal tax reform act of 1986, in relation to allocation of the unified state bond volume ceiling, and in relation to enacting the private activity bond allocation act of 2010 and providing for the expiration of certain provisions thereof
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S7422

 TITLE OF BILL :

An act relating to redistributing 2009 bond volume allocations made
pursuant to section 146 of the federal tax reform act of 1986, in
relation to allocation of the unified state bond volume ceiling, and
in relation to enacting the private activity bond allocation act of
2010 and providing for the expiration of certain provisions thereof


 PURPOSE OF THE BILL :

This bill would provide a mechanism for the orderly and efficient
tax-exempt, private activity bond allocation process for state and
local issuers by extending for an additional year to January 1,2011
the current allocation system and modifying use of bond allocations
and multi-year set asides.

 SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS :

Section 1 of the bill would set forth the title, "Private Activity
Bond Allocation Act of 2010."

Section 2 of the bill would set forth the legislative findings.

Section 3 of the bill would set forth defined terms.

Sections 4 through 6, 8 through 10 and 15 would detail the allocation
formula for the distribution of private activity bond volume ceiling
("IDB Cap"), which can be generally described as follows: one-third of
the IDB Cap is available to State agencies, one-third to local
agencies (industrial development agencies or IDAs) and one-third to a
statewide bond reserve for use by both the State and IDAs.

Section 7 of the bill would provide for certain requirements and
conditions relating to access to new employment opportunities created
in connection with industrial or manufacturing projects financed
through the issuance of qualified small issue bonds.

Section 10-a of the bill would authorize and describe the process for
future allocations of statewide ceiling for certain multi-year housing
development projects.

Sections 11 and 12 of the bill would detail provisions relating to
year end recapture of IDB Cap to the statewide bond reserve and
procedures for carryforward elections of IDB Cap, respectively.

Section 13 of the bill would create a New York State Bond Allocation
Policy Advisory Panel to provide policy advice regarding the
priorities for distribution of the statewide ceiling.

Section 14 of the bill would provide for a severability provision.

Section 16 of the bill would prohibit the proposed legislation from
superseding, altering or impairing any allocation of IDB Cap made
prior to t11e effective date of the legislation.

Section 17 of the bill would provide for an immediate effective date.

 EXISTING LAW :

Most of the provisions of the Private Activity Bond Allocation Act of
2009 shall expire on January 1, 2010.

 LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :
Similar bills have been enacted on an annual basis with respect to the
State's bond volume system. See Chapter 180 of the Laws of 2009;
Chapter 110 of the Laws of 2008; Chapter 593 of the Laws of 2007;
Chapter 228 of the Laws of 2006; Chapter 79 of the Laws of 2005;
Chapter 27 of the Laws of 2004; Chapter 32 of the Laws of 2003;
Chapter 97 of the Laws of 2002; and Chapter 15 of the Laws of 2001.

 STATEMENT IN SUPPORT :

The Federal Tax Reform Act of 1986, as amended, imposes a ceiling on
the volume of tax-exempt, private activity and certain other bonds
that may be issued in a state in any given year. It also establishes
an allocation formula which provides 50% of the statewide IDB Cap to
State agencies and the remaining 50% to local governments. New York
State has opted to establish an alternative method of distribution in
which one-third of the IDB Cap is available to State agencies,
one-third to local agencies (industrial development agencies or IDAs)
and one-third to a statewide bond reserve for use by both the State
and IDAs. Federal law permitted temporary modification of this
allocation formula by gubernatorial executive order until December 31,
1987. Following this sunset, the federal act permits states to
establish an alternative formula for allocation by statute.

The system implemented in 2000, regarding the multi-year funding of
large residential projects, as modified in the Private Activity Bond
Allocation Act of 2008, has served New York well. As development
projects grow in scale, they face increasing regulatory hurdles and
take longer to complete. Further, issuers around the state are
familiar with the process, and therefore the statutory continuation of
this approach would provide the least disruptive, most flexible and
least costly alternative for the allocation of the State's bond
volume. The multi-year provision permits more of these projects to
proceed and provides funds in the actual year it is needed. This bill
is necessary to sustain construction activity and jobs and to continue
the development of much-needed affordable housing for all New Yorkers.

In sum, this bill would continue the orderly flow of Private Activity
Bonds for the development of affordable housing and other economic
activity in New York.

 FISCAL IMPACT :

This bill would have no fiscal impact.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
This act would take effect immediately, with the following exceptions:
sections three through fourteen would expire on January 1, 2011;
except that subdivision eight of section fourteen of this act would
expire on March 1, 2011, and subdivisions two and three of section
thirteen of this act would expire on February 15, 2011. Section eleven
would continue in full force and effect and would be subject to the
applicable provisions of this act notwithstanding the expirations of
law set forth in this section.

summary: Relates to redistributing 2009 bond volume allocations, allocating the unified state bond volume ceiling, and enacting the private activity bond act of 2010.
